title: TOTP replay window is too wide: counter allows ±1 period but replay-prevention only checks current counter
description: pyotp.TOTP.verify is called with valid_window=1, which accepts codes from the previous or next 30-second slot (t-1, t, t+1). The replay-prevention counter is then set to `int(time.time()) // 30` (the current slot t). If a user legitimately uses a code from the previous slot (t-1), the counter is saved as t. An attacker who captured that code can replay it immediately because pyotp will still accept t-1 (still within the window) and the stored counter t does not block it — t-1 < t, so the counter check `counter <= user.totp_last_counter` passes as False (meaning not blocked). Concretely: attacker replays the t-1 code in the same 30-second window; `counter` is still t, stored counter is t, so `t <= t` blocks the replay — but if an attacker replays in the *next* window (t+1), `counter` becomes t+1, which is > t, so the replay succeeds because pyotp now accepts the window-1 code which maps to t (the current slot t+1 - 1). The accepted counter should be stored as `max(computed_counter_for_accepted_code, current)` across all accepted slots, not just the current slot. In practice the short window limits exposure, but a code captured during a window boundary is replayable within the adjacent window.
recommendation: Store the counter as the timecode of the *accepted code* rather than the timecode of *now*. After `pyotp.TOTP.verify(code, valid_window=1)` returns True, compute which slot was accepted by iterating t-1..t+1 and checking `pyotp.TOTP(secret).at(datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(seconds=(offset)*30)) == code` to determine `accepted_counter`, then store that. Alternatively, use `valid_window=0` (current window only, standard practice) which eliminates the ambiguity entirely and aligns with NIST recommendations.

The code at /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/auth/src/dcc_auth/routes_totp.py lines 331-338 has a genuine replay vulnerability, though the reviewer's primary attack example (t-1 code replayed in t+1) is incorrect in its specific mechanics. The real and confirmed attack path is the symmetric case:

1. A user authenticates with the **t+1** (future) code at time slot t. `totp.verify(code, valid_window=1)` accepts it (confirmed by reading pyotp source: it iterates i in range(-1, 2) = {-1, 0, +1}, so it checks timecodes t-1, t, t+1).
2. `counter = int(time.time()) // 30 = t` (current slot). Stored: `user.totp_last_counter = t`.
3. The attacker replays the same t+1 code in the next 30-second window (slot t+1). Counter is now t+1 > t (stored), so `t+1 <= t` is False — the replay-prevention check passes.
4. At time t+1, pyotp with `valid_window=1` accepts codes for t, t+1, t+2. The code is exactly for t+1, so it is accepted. **Replay succeeds.**

This was confirmed by running pyotp directly (see simulation output): `t+1 code accepted at t: True`, `At t+1: blocked=False`, `t+1 code replay accepted at t+1: True`.

So the exact textual description in the claim is imprecise, but the root cause diagnosis and fix recommendation are correct: the stored counter should be the timecode of the actually-accepted code (not always `int(time.time())//30`), or `valid_window` should be reduced to 0. The bug is real and exploitable within a 30-second boundary window whenever a future code is used.

title: Rate limiter window is reset (not counted) when expired, allowing bursts on every new window
description: In `_check_rate`, when the existing window has expired (`now - window['start'] >= seconds`) the code starts a fresh window with count=1 and immediately returns without checking the limit. This is a fixed-window counter, which has a well-known burst vulnerability: an attacker can send N requests just before a window expires (consuming the limit) and then N more immediately after the window resets, for a burst of 2N requests in a short timeframe. With `rate_limit_login = '20/minute'`, an attacker can fire 20 requests in the last seconds of minute 1 and 20 more at the start of minute 2 — 40 login attempts in a few seconds instead of 20. For login brute-force and password-reset, this doubles the effective rate. The default `rate_limit_login` of '20/minute' is per-process (noted in comments), so with multiple workers the problem compounds further.
recommendation: Use a sliding-window or token-bucket algorithm. For this in-process implementation a simple sliding window can be approximated by recording timestamps of individual requests in a deque and counting how many fall within the last `seconds` seconds. Alternatively, document the burst risk explicitly and accept it as a known limitation, but at minimum the `rate_limit_login` value should be halved to account for the window-edge burst.

When `now - window['start'] >= seconds` (window expired), the code does `bucket[ip] = {"start": now, "count": 1}` and immediately returns — it never checks `window["count"] >= n` for that first request of the new window. This is the canonical fixed-window counter algorithm with its known boundary burst: an attacker can exhaust the limit at the tail of one window and immediately fire another full quota at the start of the next window, getting 2N requests in a short span. The `rate_limit_login` default is confirmed as `"20/minute"`, so 40 login attempts are possible across a window boundary. The docstring already acknowledges the multi-worker amplification issue but says nothing about the boundary burst. No other guard exists to compensate for this — there is no sliding-window, no token bucket, no Redis back-end involved, and no secondary limit. The impact is real: brute-force protection for login, TOTP login (`rate_limit_login_totp` also `"20/minute"`), and WebAuthn login (`"20/minute"`) is effectively halved at window boundaries. The severity is medium as stated — it does not eliminate the rate limit, only doubles the effective burst.

title: ETag comparison in CRL endpoint inconsistently strips quotes on one path but not the other
description: In the Redis fast path (lines 134-138): `if if_none_match and if_none_match.strip('"') == etag_str` — this strips quotes from the incoming `If-None-Match` header and compares to the raw (unquoted) etag. In the slow DB path (line 150): `if if_none_match and if_none_match == quoted` — this compares the header directly to the quoted etag `'"<hash>"'`. Per RFC 7232, `If-None-Match` values are quoted strings. An HTTP client sending a properly-quoted `If-None-Match: "<hash>"` will: in the Redis path get 304 (correctly, because quotes are stripped before comparison); in the DB path also get 304 (correctly, because `quoted = '"<hash>"'`). However, a client sending an *unquoted* `If-None-Match: <hash>` will: in the Redis path get 304 (incorrectly accepting a non-conformant header); in the DB path get 200 (correctly rejecting a non-conformant header). The inconsistency means a compliant client always works, but a non-conformant client behaves differently depending on whether Redis is available, creating unpredictable caching behavior.
recommendation: Unify both paths: compare using `_quoted(etag_str)` on both paths, or strip quotes on both paths. The simplest fix is to use `if_none_match.strip('"') == etag_str` consistently in both the Redis and DB code paths.

verdict.reasoning: The code at /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/auth/src/dcc_auth/routes_crl.py confirms the inconsistency exactly as described. Line 137 (Redis fast path) uses `if_none_match.strip('"') == etag_str`, stripping quotes before comparison against the raw unquoted hash. Line 150 (DB slow path) uses `if_none_match == quoted` where `quoted = '"<hash>"'`, comparing directly against the quoted string. No upstream normalization exists. A compliant client sending a quoted ETag gets 304 on both paths. A non-conformant client sending an unquoted ETag gets 304 on the Redis path (line 137 strips their lack-of-quotes into a match) but 200 on the DB fallback path (line 150 requires the quotes to be present). The inconsistency is real, though limited in impact to non-conformant clients and only on the CRL endpoint.

title: In-process rate-limiter (`_check_rate`) never evicts expired entries — unbounded memory growth
description: The `_check_rate` function stores one dict entry per unique IP per rate-limit key in `app.state.rate_buckets`. Eviction only happens for the specific `(key, IP)` pair being looked up at that moment: `if window is None or now - window['start'] >= seconds`. Entries for every *other* IP are never evicted for that key. A service that receives traffic from many distinct IPs (internet-facing, behind a CDN that strips X-Forwarded-For, or during a flood) will accumulate a permanently growing dict for every rate-limit key (`login`, `register`, `totp_setup`, `user_search`, etc.). The `cred_issue` bucket in `routes_credentials.py` does iterate and prune all expired entries on every call (lines 46-48), but the shared `_check_rate` used by all other endpoints does not. Under sustained scan traffic this constitutes a slow memory leak proportional to the unique-IP count across the process lifetime, with no floor.
recommendation: Add a periodic full-sweep of expired windows either inline (e.g. when bucket size exceeds a threshold) or in the same `cleanup_loop`. At minimum, mirror the `cred_issue` pattern: before inserting a new entry, iterate and delete all windows where `now - w['start'] >= seconds`. Alternatively, replace with a Redis-backed limiter (already noted as a TODO in the comment at line 657).

The `_check_rate` function does a single `bucket.get(ip)` lookup and only resets that specific IP's window when it expires — no sweep of other IPs occurs. The shared `rate_buckets` dict therefore accumulates one entry per unique IP per rate-limit key with no global eviction. By contrast, `_check_rate_user` in routes_credentials.py:46-48 explicitly iterates all bucket entries and deletes expired ones before each call — the two implementations are inconsistent. The `cleanup_loop` in cleanup.py handles only DB token rows; it never touches `app.state.rate_buckets`. The code comment at line 665-666 acknowledges lazy per-caller eviction as a design choice but does not acknowledge the unbounded growth across unvisited IPs. The issue is real and the divergence from the `cred_issue` pattern in routes_credentials.py is clear evidence it was not intentional. Severity is appropriately medium: real memory growth under adversarial or high-diversity traffic, but not an immediate crash risk at normal scale.

title: `/.well-known/revoked-credentials` recomputes SHA-256 ETag over entire CRL on every cache miss even with Redis
description: On every request that misses the Redis-cached ETag, `_prune_and_fetch_from_redis` fetches the full sorted set (`ZRANGE 0 -1`), and `_compute_etag` sorts and SHA-256 hashes the entire list (line 66-68). Then `crl_add`/`_invalidate_etag_cache` do the same fetch+sort+hash on every new revocation. For a deployment that has revoked many credentials this is O(n) work plus a full Redis range scan triggered on every miss. Since the ETag key itself is stored in Redis and set atomically by `_invalidate_etag_cache`, the fast path (ETag key present → 304) already avoids this — the slow path only fires after the TTL-less ETag key is absent (e.g. Redis restart), but when it does fire for a large CRL it blocks on the hash computation and full ZRANGE.
recommendation: This is acceptable at small scale. If the CRL grows large, consider storing a pre-computed ETag that is invalidated lazily only on mutations and set with a long TTL, so a Redis restart does not force a full recompute on the next request.

The ETAG_KEY has no TTL (plain `redis.set` at line 143 and 192), confirming it persists until Redis restart or mutation. title: TOTP verify-setup does not initialize totp_last_counter, enabling same-code reuse during short replay window

title: SMTP STARTTLS used without certificate verification (potential MITM on outbound email)
description: The `_send_smtp_sync` function calls `s.starttls()` with no arguments. Python's `smtplib.SMTP.starttls()` defaults to an SSLContext with `check_hostname=False` and `verify_mode=ssl.CERT_NONE` when no context is passed. This means TLS is established but the server's certificate is not validated, allowing a network-path attacker to MITM the TLS session and intercept password-reset tokens and email verification links in transit. The `SMTP_SSL` path for port-465 has the same issue — `smtplib.SMTP_SSL()` also defaults to no-verify when no context is given.
recommendation: Create an explicit `ssl.create_default_context()` and pass it as the `context=` argument to both `SMTP_SSL()` and `starttls()`. This enables certificate verification and hostname checking by default.

Runtime inspection of the installed Python stdlib confirms that both methods fall through to `ssl._create_stdlib_context()` when no context is provided, and that context has `check_hostname=False` and `verify_mode=0` (i.e. `ssl.CERT_NONE`). TLS is negotiated but the server certificate is never validated and hostname is not checked, making a network-path MITM trivially feasible. There is no compensating guard elsewhere in the file or in the call chain. The fix is straightforward: pass `context=ssl.create_default_context()` to both `SMTP_SSL()` and `starttls()`.

title: Plaintext recovery tokens logged to service log when SMTP is unconfigured

title: cert-login rate-limiter uses leftmost X-Forwarded-For, trivially bypassed by spoofed header

title: GRANT_ALL_SAFE sets all reserved permission bits, contradicting its stated security guarantee

This claim is false. `(1 << 52) - 1` is a bitmask with all 52 bits set, including 27 reserved bit positions (5–7, 13–19, 28–29, 37–50). When a developer adds a new permission in any of these reserved slots — trusting the documented guarantee — every existing owner/ADMINISTRATOR-role holder silently gains that permission the moment the constant is referenced through `calculate_guild_permissions` or `calculate_channel_permissions`. A developer writing `if has_permission(perms, Permissions.NEW_DANGEROUS_OP)` to gate a sensitive action would find that all admins and guild owners already pass the check without any explicit grant. The only bits that are protected are those at position 52 and above. The intended behaviour would require `GRANT_ALL_SAFE` to be computed as the OR of only the currently-defined `Permissions` members.

title: apply_atomic_update returns default_state on rollback with no error signal, causing false broadcast

title: Two separate DB connections per plugin op: gate session and handler session
description: Every plugin op (e.g. tamagotchi:feed) acquires two separate DB connections sequentially. The gate in ws_ops.py opens `gate_session` (line 128–135), runs `is_guild_member` + `is_plugin_enabled_for_guild`, then closes it. The tamagotchi handler then opens a second session inside `_handle_action` (plugins/tamagotchi/backend.py:203) for `apply_atomic_update`. Connection acquisition from the asyncpg pool is cheap but non-zero: each acquisition involves a round-trip through the pool and potentially a new TLS handshake to Postgres. Under rapid repeated plugin ops (multiple users clicking feed simultaneously) this doubles pool pressure relative to what a single reused session could achieve. The WS op gate already has the membership result; passing the open session to the handler would eliminate the second acquisition.

The claim of "a round-trip through the pool and potentially a new TLS handshake to Postgres" is incorrect for asyncpg connection pools — pool checkouts are in-memory operations against pre-established physical connections; no TLS handshake occurs per checkout. The real overhead is two asyncio context manager enter/exit cycles and two pool checkout/checkin pairs, which is cheap. The fix proposed (threading the gate session into the handler) would be a valid micro-optimization but the severity is low, not medium.

On a self-host server, the owner/admin is identified via the ready-frame is_admin flag stored in serverAdmin (cert-login users have no cloud is_admin). title: Pre-ready event buffer cleared before hello/version check completes

The close handler fires _scheduleReconnect if wantConnected is true. The close event happens synchronously after the close() call on the WebSocket from within the message handler. On the reconnect attempt, connect() creates a new _readyPromise but any caller that already resolved their waitForReady() via the finally-block fallback (line 169-172 — triggered because _readyDone is false when _dial throws or the socket closes before ready) will not get a subsequent notification. For a too-old server, gapFillAll will fire HTTP requests with the valid token to an incompatible server — the requests will succeed (the REST API is separate from the WS) but the gap-fill data is redundant. This is a minor wasted request, not a correctness issue for the data, but it is wasted I/O and a logic gap.

title: idb-shared: openIdentityDb rejects on IDB blocked but IDBDatabase is not closed

title: 1 Hz polling loop always rebuilds and reassigns reactive state even when nothing changed
description: `ServerStateMirror.refresh()` runs every 1 second via `setInterval`. On every tick it builds a new `next` object and assigns `this.byId = next`, unconditionally triggering Svelte's reactive diffing pipeline. When the connection states have not changed (the common steady-state), this still allocates a new plain object and forces Svelte to walk all reactive subscribers. With multiple servers in the pool this occurs for every server entry on every tick.

A shallow string-compare on `state` (which is a string union) and a reference-compare on `helloMeta` (null or an object set once on hello) is sufficient and avoids allocation on steady-state ticks.

title: Repeated open/close of IndexedDB connection for every identity read/write operation

On `onversionchange` or `onblocked` events, null the cache and reopen. The impact is real: latency is added on every login on any device, and is worse under IDB contention (e.g. Service Worker) or on slow mobile storage.

title: Cloud JWT access and refresh tokens stored in localStorage — fully readable by XSS
description: Both `access_token` and `refresh_token` are persisted in `localStorage` under the keys `dcc.tokens.access` and `dcc.tokens.refresh`. Unlike `HttpOnly` cookies, `localStorage` is readable by any JavaScript executing on the same origin. A single XSS vulnerability anywhere in the SvelteKit application allows an attacker to exfiltrate both tokens and use them to take over the victim's cloud account, issue new certs, read messages, and impersonate the user until the refresh token is revoked. The comment in storage.ts acknowledges the tradeoff ("localStorage works fine") but does not capture this risk.
recommendation: Store the refresh token in an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie set by the auth-svc on login, and keep only the short-lived access token in memory (not localStorage). If cross-tab token sharing is needed, use the Web Locks + BroadcastChannel pattern instead of localStorage. At minimum, ensure CSP headers on howispulse.com are strict enough to make XSS execution very difficult.

The only `HttpOnly` cookie (`pulse_session`) is used exclusively for cert-credential endpoints in `credentials.ts`, not for the main cloud auth tokens. The production Caddyfile snippet (`infra/prod/Caddyfile.pulse.snippet`) contains only a plain `reverse_proxy pulse_web:80` directive with no CSP response headers. The only CSP present is a meta-tag in `app.html` that includes `script-src 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'`, rendering it nearly useless against XSS. There is no existing guard (HttpOnly cookie, memory-only storage, strict CSP) that would mitigate XSS-based token theft. An XSS payload can trivially call `localStorage.getItem('dcc.tokens.access')` and `localStorage.getItem('dcc.tokens.refresh')` and exfiltrate both, giving an attacker a 30-day refresh token valid for the cloud account.

title: Unvalidated deserialization of `isCloud` flag from localStorage enables cloud-JWT forwarding to attacker origins after XSS
description: `loadFromStorage()` does `return parsed as ServerEntry[]` — a TypeScript type assertion with no runtime field validation. The `isCloud` boolean controls which bearer token is used (`bearerFor` at `client.ts:179`) and how the request URL is built (`buildUrl` at `client.ts:89-95`). An XSS attacker who can write to `localStorage` (trivially possible if XSS is achieved) can inject a crafted `pulse.servers` entry with `isCloud: false` and `hostname: https://attacker.com`. Any subsequent `request()` or `requestForm()` call that routes to that `serverId` will prepend the attacker's origin to the path and send the self-host session token there. For the reverse direction, injecting `isCloud: true` with a real non-cloud hostname still results in relative-path requests to the current origin (the built-in `isCloud` path override in `buildUrl` wins), but the absence of runtime validation is the root cause that would make future code changes silently dangerous.
recommendation: In `loadFromStorage()` / `init()`, re-derive `isCloud` from the stored `hostname` (compare against `CLOUD_HOSTNAME`) rather than trusting the stored boolean. Add a migration step that normalises existing stored entries on startup.

verdict.reasoning:
The code defect is real: `loadFromStorage()` at line 73 does `return parsed as ServerEntry[]` with no runtime validation, so a crafted `pulse.servers` entry injected into localStorage survives into `serversStore.servers` unmodified. Both `buildUrl` (line 91) and `bearerFor` (line 179) branch on the untrusted `server.isCloud` value.

However, the claimed impact — forwarding a cloud JWT to an attacker origin — is not reachable via this path. `bearerFor` sends the cloud JWT only when `server.isCloud === true`, and `buildUrl` with `isCloud: true` always returns a relative path (line 91: `server.isCloud` → `return ep + path`), so injecting `isCloud: true` with an attacker hostname still sends the request to the current origin.

The realistic attack with `isCloud: false, hostname: attacker.com`: `bearerFor` calls `sessionTokens.get(server.id)` using the injected fake `id`. A freshly injected fake entry has no matching session token, so `bearerFor` returns `null` and `request()` throws `SessionExpiredError` before the fetch fires. To leak an actual self-host session token this way, the attacker would need to inject an `id` that matches an existing entry in `sessionTokens` — possible if the attacker can also read localStorage to learn the real `id`, but at that point the session token in `sessionTokens` is already directly accessible (session tokens are themselves in localStorage or in-memory state that XSS can read directly).

The `auth` endpoint always routes to cloud-relative regardless of `isCloud` (line 213: `endpoint === 'auth'` forces `resolveServer(undefined, true)`), so the `hasCloud = stored.some(s => s.isCloud)` bootstrap logic can be spoofed by injecting a fake cloud entry — but again this only produces relative-path requests.

Summary: the missing runtime validation of `isCloud` is a genuine code quality issue and a latent future-hazard (as the reviewer notes), but the concrete exploit path for exfiltrating a cloud JWT to an attacker origin is not reachable given the current code structure. Any XSS attacker who can write localStorage can already read it too, making the token directly accessible without this indirection. The `add()` method correctly re-derives `isCloud` from hostname comparison — the fix should be applied in `loadFromStorage()` / `init()` as recommended, but the severity is low rather than high because exploitation requires XSS and the token exfiltration path is blocked by the `isCloud → relative URL` invariant in `buildUrl`.

title: applyNoiseFilter: concurrent calls race on #sendProcessorMode, installing two processors
description: When setMicEnabled(true) runs, it awaits setMicrophoneEnabled(), which causes LiveKit to fire RoomEvent.LocalTrackPublished synchronously before the promise resolves. The LocalTrackPublished handler immediately calls 'void this.applyNoiseFilter()' (fire-and-forget). Once setMicrophoneEnabled() resolves, setMicEnabled continues and itself calls 'await this.applyNoiseFilter()'. Both calls therefore proceed to createSendProcessor() and then await audioTrack.setProcessor(handle.processor), calling setProcessor twice. The first processor (with its AudioContext, WASM instance, and RNNoise worklet) is orphaned without being destroyed: its destroy() is never called, leaking an AudioContext and WASM memory for every mic enable. Additionally the second setProcessor() call replaces the first but the first processor's level-tap RAF loop is never cancelled, so #onSendLevel continues to fire from the leaked processor.

Before entering the async body, check the flag; set it on entry, clear it in a finally block. Alternatively, remove the 'void this.applyNoiseFilter()' from the LocalTrackPublished handler (line 843) since setMicEnabled already calls applyNoiseFilter after setMicrophoneEnabled returns — the event handler call is redundant and is the root cause of the race.

Then `publishTrack` returns, `setMicrophoneEnabled` resolves, `setMicEnabled` continues at line 374 and calls `await this.applyNoiseFilter()` — a second invocation. The `handle.setLevelTap(this.#onSendLevel)` RAF loop from the first processor also remains active because `#onSendLevel` is only cleared via `#resetSendLevel()` which is not called. title: RemoteAudioElements.#ensureContext does not check AudioContext.state before reusing it

title: setPttMode(off) unconditionally enables the mic, ignoring admin force-mute override

If an admin has force-muted the local user and the user switches out of PTT mode (e.g., via the settings panel), their mic becomes enabled despite the admin override. toggleMic() and pttPress() both respect the override, but setPttMode(false) does not.
recommendation: Add the same guard to setPttMode: 'if (!on && this.#selfOverride().muted) { settings.setPttMode(false); return; }' — or refactor so setPttMode delegates through toggleMic / a shared helper that enforces the override.

title: Full array spread-copy on every speaking-state change at RAF cadence
description: Each time a remote participant's speaking state transitions, `#onRemoteSpeakingChange` allocates a new array (`[...this.participants]`) and a new plain object (`{ ...copy[idx] }`) to satisfy Svelte's reactive mutation detection (lines 1078-1080). At 60 fps with N active speakers this is N array copies × N elements per frame. The same pattern appears in `#setLocalSpeaking` (lines 1088-1090) and in `#patchAudioLevels` (line 992). These copies are all avoidable: Svelte 5 Runes track `$state` arrays by value identity but individual element mutation on a `$state<VoiceParticipant[]>` can be made reactive by making each VoiceParticipant itself a `$state` object, so only the changed participant triggers a re-render rather than the whole list being replaced.
recommendation: Make each `VoiceParticipant` a reactive object (e.g. wrap in a class with `$state` fields, or use `SvelteMap`). Then mutate `.isSpeaking` and `.audioLevel` directly on the participant object; Svelte 5 will only invalidate components reading that participant's fields instead of re-rendering the entire participants list on every speaking transition.

verdict.reasoning:
The code at the referenced lines does exactly what the reviewer describes, but with one important correction to the severity framing.

**What the code actually does:**

1. `#onRemoteSpeakingChange` (lines 1075-1081): On each speaking-state transition, allocates `[...this.participants]` (full array copy) and then `{ ...copy[idx], isSpeaking: speaking }` (object spread). This fires via `RemoteSpeakingTracker`'s `#onChange` callback.

2. `#setLocalSpeaking` (lines 1083-1092): Same two-allocation pattern on local speaking transitions.

3. `#patchAudioLevels` (line 992): Does `this.participants = [...this.participants]` when any `audioLevel` or `isSpeaking` differs. This runs via `setInterval(..., 200)` — **every 200 ms, not at 60 fps / RAF cadence**.

**Important correction to the reviewer's claim:** The reviewer says `#patchAudioLevels` runs "at 60 fps" and "at RAF cadence". This is wrong — it uses `setInterval` at 200 ms (5 Hz), not `requestAnimationFrame`. The RAF loop is in `RemoteSpeakingTracker` itself (per-participant audio analysis), but the `#patchAudioLevels` allocation only happens 5 times per second, not 60.

**However, the `#onRemoteSpeakingChange` issue is real and does fire from a RAF loop:** `RemoteSpeakingTracker.attach()` runs a `requestAnimationFrame` loop per remote participant. The `SpeakingDetector.feed()` is called each RAF frame. When `SpeakingDetector` detects a state change, it calls `#onChange` synchronously inside the RAF callback, which calls `#onRemoteSpeakingChange`, which does both allocations inside the RAF loop. The hysteresis (300 ms hold, -55/-65 dBFS thresholds) means the callback fires infrequently in practice — only on true speaking transitions — not every frame. So "N copies per frame" is an overstatement: it's N copies per speaking-state-transition, which is rate-limited by the hysteresis logic.

**Verdict:** The pattern is real — immutable-style array replacement is used where direct mutation would work with Svelte 5 `$state`. The allocations occur at speaking transitions (event-driven, infrequent due to hysteresis) and at 200 ms intervals for audio levels. The "60 fps × N speakers" framing overstates the actual frequency. The fix recommendation (per-participant `$state` objects) is valid and would eliminate the full-list copy on each change. This is a genuine but low-to-medium severity inefficiency — it causes GC pressure on speaking transitions and a full list copy every 200 ms while in voice, but not the continuous per-frame allocation the reviewer implies.

title: Redundant 200 ms setInterval poll for values already pushed via event/RAF callbacks
description: `#patchAudioLevels` runs every 200 ms (line 967) and checks `p.audioLevel` and `this.#remoteSpeaking.isSpeaking()` for every participant. The `isSpeaking` check in the poll is similarly redundant because `#onRemoteSpeakingChange` already updates it in real time via the RAF callbacks in `RemoteSpeakingTracker`. The net result is that the poll loop at 5 Hz iterates over all participants and does an O(1) Map lookup per participant that almost always finds no change — wasted work proportional to participant count, running continuously for the entire duration of a voice session.
recommendation: Remove the `setInterval` polling for `isSpeaking` — it is already driven in real time. If the server-side `audioLevel` value is actually needed in the UI, hook `RoomEvent.ActiveSpeakersChanged` directly (it already triggers `#scheduleRefresh`) and read `audioLevel` there. If `audioLevel` is not rendered anywhere meaningful, remove it from `VoiceParticipant` entirely.

title: One separate requestAnimationFrame loop per remote participant in RemoteSpeakingTracker
description: Each `attach()` call spawns its own independent `requestAnimationFrame` loop (lines 63-70). With N remote participants there are N separate RAF registrations fired every frame. Each reads 512 floats via `getFloatTimeDomainData` and computes an RMS. All entries share the same `AudioContext`, so the analyser reads are cheap relative to the RAF overhead itself, but N separate browser RAF callbacks (each going through the JS scheduler, closure captures, and a Map write) still add up. At 10 participants this is 10 individual RAF callbacks per frame = 600 scheduler entries per second from speaking detection alone.
recommendation: Consolidate into a single shared RAF loop inside `RemoteSpeakingTracker` that iterates over `#entries` in one pass per frame, similar to how `LocalMicAnalyser` uses a single `#loop`. This reduces RAF registrations from O(N) to O(1) and keeps all analyser reads batched in one tick.

Each `attach()` call creates a new closure `loop` and schedules it with `requestAnimationFrame(loop)` (line 70). The loop reschedules itself each frame via `entry.raf = requestAnimationFrame(loop)` (line 68). There is no shared loop, no consolidation guard, and no existing mechanism that batches these. With N remote participants, N independent RAF chains run every frame. The `Entry` type even stores a per-entry `raf: number | null` field (line 19), confirming the design is intentionally one-RAF-per-participant. `LocalMicAnalyser` confirms the contrasting pattern: it has a single `#loop` class method with a single `#raf` field, exactly as the reviewer describes. The impact path is fully reachable — any voice channel with multiple remote participants triggers it. The severity "low" is appropriate because typical participant counts are small and the per-frame work (512-sample RMS) is modest, but the O(N) RAF registration pattern is a genuine inefficiency that could be consolidated into O(1) with a single shared loop iterating over `#entries`.

title: Admin force-deafen is purely client-side: tampered client can hear channel audio despite server-side override
description: When an admin force-deafens a participant via the voice_override WS event, the enforcement is entirely client-side: the handler calls voice.setDeafened(true), which mutes the local audio output and disables the deafen toggle in the UI. A user running a modified client (or who intercepts the WS message) can simply skip the setDeafened call and continue receiving and playing all subscribed audio tracks. LiveKit's permission model does not gate inbound subscriptions server-side, only outbound publishes — so there is no server-enforced mechanism to prevent the deafened participant from hearing the room. The comment in voice.ts line 48 acknowledges this explicitly ('a tampered client could still play subscribed audio — same trust model as Discord's server-deafen'). Force-mute, by contrast, is hard-enforced via LiveKit publish-permission grants set in the token and updated via livekit_client.update_participant. The practical impact is that in any scenario where an admin intends to prevent a user from gaining information from voice channel content (e.g., confidential discussion, moderation session), force-deafen provides no actual enforcement guarantee against a determined user.
recommendation: Document this limitation clearly in admin-facing UI so moderators understand force-deafen is a UX/UI gate only, not a security control. If true enforcement is needed, the only option is to remove the user from the room entirely (force-disconnect, which is already implemented via voice_disconnect). Consider adding a UI note on the force-deafen action: 'User can still hear channel audio on modified clients; use Disconnect to fully remove them.'

verdict.reasoning: The code confirms the claim precisely. In `web/src/lib/ws/handlers/voice.ts` lines 45-52, the comment explicitly states "a tampered client could still play subscribed audio — same trust model as Discord's server-deafen." The backend `voice_override.py` lines 104-107 also documents this: "Live LiveKit update is only meaningful for the mute side — the deafen enforcement is client-only (LiveKit doesn't gate inbound subscriptions by participant permission). Skip the LiveKit call if mute wasn't part of this patch." In `livekit_client.py`, `_livekit_update_participant` always sets `can_subscribe=True` and has no mechanism to revoke inbound subscriptions — it only controls `can_publish` and `can_publish_sources`. The token issuance in `token.py` also hardcodes `can_subscribe=True`. Force-mute is properly server-enforced via LiveKit publish-permission grants; force-deafen is purely a UI/client-side gate. A user running a modified client can skip the `voice.setDeafened` call in the WS handler and continue hearing all subscribed audio. However, this is a known, intentional design decision already documented in code comments (not an undetected bug), and the severity is low because: (a) it mirrors Discord's explicit design choice, (b) the alternative (force-disconnect via `voice_disconnect`) already exists for true enforcement, and (c) the application is not positioning force-deafen as a security control against determined adversaries.

title: channelPermissions.resolveForUser ignores serverAdmin — self-host admins never get GRANT_ALL_SAFE at channel scope
description: Line 64 hardcodes `const isAdmin = !!auth.user?.is_admin;` to determine whether the current user is a global admin before running the channel-permission resolver. On a self-host instance, a cert-login user's admin status does NOT come from `auth.user.is_admin` (that field reflects the cloud auth /me response). Instead it comes from the `ready` frame via the `serverAdmin` store, keyed by server ID. Because `channelPermissions.svelte.ts` never imports `activeServer` or `serverAdmin`, a self-host server admin (non-owner) always evaluates `isAdmin = false`. The resolver then proceeds through the full role+overwrite path, and if that admin holds no explicit guild roles, they will not receive `GRANT_ALL_SAFE`. In practice, UI permission gates backed by `hasChannelPermission` — `HqStreamButton` (STREAM), `ScreenShareModeButton` (STREAM), `VoiceControlBar` (USE_VIDEO) — will appear disabled or hidden for the self-host admin even though the backend will permit the actions. By contrast `roles.recomputeGuild` (line 138-141) already applies the correct dual-path logic (`srv?.isCloud ? auth.user?.is_admin : serverAdmin.isAdmin(serverId)`). Guild owners are not affected because `isOwner` is derived directly from `guild.owner_id === me`, which is correct.
recommendation: Mirror the pattern used in `roles.recomputeGuild`: import `activeServer` and `serverAdmin` into `channelPermissions.svelte.ts` and replace line 64 with `const isAdmin = activeServer.current?.isCloud ? !!auth.user?.is_admin : serverAdmin.isAdmin(activeServer.serverId);`.

In `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/web/src/lib/stores/channelPermissions.svelte.ts` line 64, `const isAdmin = !!auth.user?.is_admin;` always reads the cloud auth field. For a self-host cert-login admin, `auth.user` holds the cert-login session user, and `is_admin` on that object reflects the cloud account's admin status, not the per-server admin status set from the `ready` frame. The `serverAdmin` store (which holds the per-server admin flag keyed by serverId, fed from the `ready` frame) is never consulted here. By contrast, `roles.svelte.ts` lines 138-141 already applies the correct dual-path logic: `const isAdmin = srv?.isCloud ? !!auth.user?.is_admin : serverAdmin.isAdmin(activeServer.serverId);`. Since `resolveChannelPermissions` in `bitfield.ts` line 112 short-circuits to `GRANT_ALL_SAFE` only when `isGlobalAdmin || isOwner`, a self-host cert-login admin (non-owner) will evaluate `isAdmin = false`, skip the short-circuit, and proceed through the full role+overwrite evaluation path. If that admin holds no explicit guild roles with the required bits, `hasChannelPermission` will return false. All three affected UI gates (`HqStreamButton` line 40, `ScreenShareModeButton` line 43, `VoiceControlBar` line 37) call `channelPermissions.hasChannelPermission`, making the impact path fully reachable. Guild owners are not affected because `isOwner` is derived from `guild.owner_id === me` which is correct.

title: O(guilds × channels) flat-scan to resolve channel's guild in three reactive derived expressions

Every time `guilds.channelsByGuild`, `voice.channelId`, or any other reactive dependency changes, each component allocates a new flat array from all guild channels and scans it linearly. For a user in many guilds with many channels this is wasteful and runs on every WS event that touches channel state.

title: resolveChannelPermissions rebuilds the overwrites array and runs isSorted on every reactive call
description: `resolveForUser` is called from `hasChannelPermission`, which is invoked inside `$derived.by` blocks in multiple components. The snapshots and their bigint conversions are recomputed from scratch even though the underlying data (channel overwrites and user roles) is unlikely to have changed. The role snapshots are already cached in `RoleStore._snapshotsCache` (already sorted after `recomputeGuild`), but the overwrite-to-snapshot conversion and the `isSorted` O(r) check inside `resolveChannelPermissions` are repeated on every reactive read of `hasChannelPermission`.
recommendation: Cache the resolved bigint per (channelId, userId, rolesHash) inside `ChannelPermissionsStore`, invalidating only when `apply()` is called (new overwrites pushed from WS) or `roles.recomputeGuild` fires. Alternatively, pre-convert and store `OverwriteSnapshot[]` in `byChannel` instead of raw `Overwrite[]`, avoiding the `toBitfield` loop on every reactive read. The `isSorted` path is already optimised for the cached case via `_snapshotsCache`, so no change needed there.

The roles side is already optimized — `roles.snapshotsForUser` returns `_snapshotsCache` built by `recomputeGuild` — but the overwrite-to-snapshot conversion is not cached anywhere in `ChannelPermissionsStore`. The claim correctly identifies all three points: the `.map()` + `toBitfield` loop on overwrites, the `isSorted` O(r) traversal, and the fact that role snapshots are already cached. title: discoverPlugins does an O(n×m) inner scan to match manifests to entry paths
description: Inside `discoverPlugins`, for each of the `n` discovered manifest paths the code runs `Object.keys(entryModules).find(p => nameFromPath(p) === dirName)` — a linear scan over all `m` entry-module paths. This is O(n×m) overall. Both `Object.keys(entryModules)` and `nameFromPath` are called fresh per outer iteration; `nameFromPath` itself runs a regex match on every candidate. However `discoverPlugins` is called from `loadAll` at app boot and is also exported for potential use in admin UI, so as the plugin count grows this compounds. Additionally the `nameFromPath` regex is re-applied to every entry path for every manifest.

title: channelPermissions resolver uses cloud-only admin flag on self-host instances
description: resolveForUser() reads isAdmin as !!auth.user?.is_admin unconditionally. On a self-host server, the cert-login owner has auth.user === null (there is no cloud /me call), so is_admin is always undefined → false regardless of the serverAdmin store. Consequently, hasChannelPermission() returns the wrong bitfield for a self-host admin: instead of GRANT_ALL_SAFE, the resolver falls through to the role-based path, which typically grants no special access. In practice this hides the HQ-stream button (Perm.STREAM, HqStreamButton.svelte:40), the screen-share mode button (Perm.STREAM, ScreenShareModeButton.svelte:43), and the video button (Perm.USE_VIDEO, VoiceControlBar.svelte:37) for the self-host owner. The backend enforces permissions independently, so this is a UI privilege understatement rather than a privilege escalation — but an admin who cannot see the streaming/video controls on their own server is a functional regression with a security dimension: the admin loses UI affordances gated on channel-level ACLs that they legitimately own. By contrast, roles.svelte.ts:139-141 uses the correct two-branch check (cloud → auth.user?.is_admin, self-host → serverAdmin.isAdmin(activeServer.serverId)).
recommendation: Import activeServer and serverAdmin into channelPermissions.svelte.ts and mirror the same branch used in roles.svelte.ts recomputeGuild(): const srv = activeServer.current; const isAdmin = srv?.isCloud ? !!auth.user?.is_admin : serverAdmin.isAdmin(activeServer.serverId);. title: Viewer manual pause suppressed by unconditional syncingUntil update in syncSoft
description: syncSoft() sets `syncingUntil = Date.now() + SYNC_QUIET_MS` (2000 ms) unconditionally before calling corrector.applySoft(). When the host is playing and drift is within the 0.1 s tolerance, applySoft returns 'none' — no seek or nudge is issued — but syncingUntil is still advanced. The heartbeat interval is 3000 ms, so a new 2 s suppression window is opened every 3 s. handleEvent() at line 267 suppresses any viewer 'pause' or 'play' event that arrives while `now < syncingUntil`. Because the suppression window (2 s) overlaps with heartbeats (3 s) by 2/3, roughly two out of every three manual pause attempts by the viewer are silently dropped: the event is swallowed, `viewerPaused` stays false, and the next heartbeat calls syncSoft again, renewing the window. The viewer cannot reliably pause a smoothly-running watch party stream.
recommendation: Only advance syncingUntil when applySoft (or applyHard) actually took a corrective action. Move `syncingUntil = Date.now() + SYNC_QUIET_MS` into the branches of syncSoft/syncHard that return an action other than 'none', or check the return value of corrector.applySoft() before setting syncingUntil.

verdict.reasoning:
The code confirms the claim. In `syncSoft()` at line 139 of WatchPartyTile.svelte, `syncingUntil = Date.now() + SYNC_QUIET_MS` (2000ms) is set unconditionally before `corrector.applySoft()` is called. The return value of `applySoft` is only logged; it is never checked to decide whether to advance `syncingUntil`.

`applySoft()` in sync.ts returns `'none'` in two cases: (1) host is paused (`!state.is_playing`, line 110), or (2) drift is within the 0.1s noise floor (`abs < DRIFT_IGNORE_S`, line 119). In the steady-state scenario described — host playing, viewer in sync — every heartbeat (every 3000ms) calls `syncSoft`, which unconditionally opens a 2000ms suppression window regardless of outcome.

`handleEvent` at line 267 suppresses any viewer `'pause'` or `'play'` event arriving while `now < syncingUntil`. Since the window covers 2000ms out of every 3000ms cycle (2/3 of the time), a manual pause attempt that falls in the first 2s after any heartbeat is silently dropped: the event is swallowed, `viewerPaused` stays `false`, and the next heartbeat re-enters `syncSoft`, resetting the window.

The component's own comment at lines 108-117 asserts "2000ms < heartbeat interval (3000ms) so legitimate manual play/pause outside the post-sync echo window still works" — but this is precisely the reasoning flaw: it assumes suppression only happens after an actual corrective action, whereas the code sets the window even when `applySoft` returns `'none'`. The fix is to move `syncingUntil = Date.now() + SYNC_QUIET_MS` to after checking the return value of `applySoft`/`applyHard`, setting it only when the action is not `'none'`.

title: DetachedWatchParties poll timer runs unconditionally from construction, never stopped
description: The DetachedWatchParties constructor starts `setInterval(() => this.#sweepClosedWindows(), 800)` unconditionally and never calls clearInterval on it. In contrast, DetachedStreams (detach.svelte.ts) starts the poll lazily only when the first popup window is opened, and stops it when all windows are closed. Since detachedWatchParties is a module-level singleton, the 800 ms interval fires for the entire lifetime of the page even when no watch-party popup has ever been opened. #sweepClosedWindows iterates over #windows (which is empty) on every tick — wasted work, and the timer is a resource that can never be GC'd.

title: connectWhep: onTrack never fires if incoming tracks carry no stream association, leaving player stuck in 'playing' phase with blank video

title: N+1 DB sessions in push fan-out: one session opened per mentioned user
description: `fan_out_mention_push` spawns one `asyncio.gather` task per mentioned user, and each task opens a fresh `SessionLocal()` to call `send_push_to_user`. `send_push_to_user` issues a `SELECT … WHERE user_id = <uid>` then a conditional `DELETE`/`UPDATE`. The pool default (typically 5–10 connections) means hundreds of tasks will queue behind the pool semaphore, stalling the request worker for the duration of all push round-trips.
recommendation: Batch all subscriptions in a single query: `SELECT * FROM chat.web_push_subscriptions WHERE user_id = ANY(:ids)`, group by user, then call the existing `_send_one` threads concurrently. If `fan_out_mention_push` is called with 500 user IDs (e.g., @everyone in a large guild), all 500 `_push_one` coroutines race to acquire a connection simultaneously. The first 30 get through; the remaining 470 queue behind the pool semaphore waiting for connections to be released.

The reviewer's severity assessment (high) is accurate for large guilds. The recommendation to batch into `SELECT ... WHERE user_id = ANY(:ids)` and one session would collapse N sessions+queries to 1–2 regardless of recipient count.

title: `StreamChatOverlay`: O(n) filter + Set rebuild on every reactive update

title: `fan_out_mention_push` blocks the POST /messages response until all push round-trips complete

title: `youtubeTitle` cache never evicted: unbounded memory growth across watch-party sessions

title: WHEP resource URL (Location header) accepted from server without origin validation — open redirect on teardown DELETE

If the server (or a MITM on the unencrypted localhost:8889 path in development, or a misconfigured MEDIAMTX_PUBLIC_BASE) returns an absolute `Location` value pointing to an arbitrary host, the teardown `DELETE` at line 110 will be sent to that attacker-controlled URL, leaking the `Origin` header and potentially hitting internal infrastructure. In production the WHEP endpoint is behind HTTPS/TLS so the risk is lower, but the local dev path (`http://localhost:8889`) is plaintext and a compromised MediaMTX response could redirect the DELETE to any host. There is no validation that the resolved `resourceUrl` shares the same origin as `whepUrl`.

title: Native watch-party URL SSRF via DNS rebinding — `_is_private_host` only blocks IP literals

It blocks IP literals and well-known localhost names but explicitly cannot resolve hostnames ('We cannot do DNS resolution here', line 213). An attacker can register a public DNS name that resolves to `10.0.0.1`, `192.168.x.x`, `169.254.169.254` (cloud metadata), etc. The parsed URL is stored in Redis and broadcast verbatim to all channel members as `{type:'native', url}`. The `NativeVideoPlayer.svelte` component then sets `src={source.url}` on a `<video>` element. Every viewer's browser will then make a credentialed fetch to the private address, leaking cookies/auth tokens or probing the internal network. The attack requires channel membership (to call `watch_start` on the WS) but that bar is low on an open instance.
recommendation: Either (a) disable native URL support entirely if it is not core functionality, (b) maintain a strict allowlist of allowed URL prefixes (no arbitrary third-party HTTPS), or (c) perform server-side DNS resolution at parse time to block RFC-1918/link-local addresses. Option (c) must be done asynchronously and cached with a short TTL, and must handle CNAMEs.

At `/watch_source.py` lines 212-216, `_is_private_host` explicitly documents its own limitation: "We cannot do DNS resolution here … so we only block the obvious literal forms above." For a hostname like `internal.attacker.com` that resolves to `10.0.0.1`, `ipaddress.ip_address(hostname)` raises `ValueError` and the function returns `False`, allowing the URL through. The parsed `{"type": "native", "url": url}` is stored verbatim in Redis and broadcast to all channel members via the `watch_state` op. `NativeVideoPlayer.svelte` (line 82) then sets `src={source.url}` directly on a `<video>` element. title: Attachment MIME type is not validated against an allowlist — arbitrary MIME stored and used as Content-Type for presigned PUT
description: The `AttachmentUploadIn.mime` field accepts any string up to 128 characters (schema line 186). The value is stored verbatim in the database and forwarded as the `ContentType` parameter to `presigned_put_url`. MinIO enforces that the PUT's `Content-Type` header matches the signed value, but the attacker controls what that signed value is. A malicious client can claim `mime='text/html'` for any upload. The presigned GET URL issued later will include `Content-Type: text/html` in its signed response headers, causing the browser to render the fetched object as HTML. If that object is then served inline on the Pulse origin (`https://howispulse.com/...`), this creates a stored-XSS vector via the attachment. The `_is_inline_mime` function at line 211 does control the `Content-Disposition` (inline vs attachment) on download re-signing, but it relies on the caller-supplied MIME, not a server-verified one.
recommendation: Validate `mime` against an explicit allowlist of safe values (e.g., `image/*`, `video/*`, `audio/*`, `application/pdf`, etc.) and reject or normalise anything outside it. Do not trust the client's MIME claim for deciding Content-Type in presigned URLs.

The value flows directly into `presigned_put_url(..., content_type=payload.mime, ...)` at `attachments.py:159`, which sets `ContentType` in the S3 params (s3.py line 136). MinIO stores the object with that `Content-Type`. The presigned GET URL path (`presigned_get_url` in s3.py) does NOT pass a `ResponseContentType` override, so MinIO returns the attacker-controlled MIME verbatim. The nginx config at `infra/prod/web-nginx.conf` (lines 137–149) proxies `/pulse-attachments/*` to MinIO under the `howispulse.com` origin (confirmed by `.env.example`: `S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT=https://howispulse.com`), with no Content-Type header override. The `_is_inline_mime` function at line 211 does return `False` for `text/html`, which causes `Content-Disposition: attachment` on the download-url re-sign endpoint — this partially mitigates but does not eliminate the issue because: (1) the initial presigned PUT URL path does not set any Content-Disposition, (2) `Content-Disposition: attachment` does not prevent the browser from using the MIME type in some contexts, and (3) the raw presigned GET URL (e.g. from MinIO directly) would still serve `text/html` inline. The complete exploit chain is reachable: malicious client claims `mime='text/html'`, uploads any content, and the stored object is served as HTML from the Pulse origin.

title: GuildSettingsDialog: permission-change WS event resets the active tab while the dialog is open

title: VoiceChannelView: PTT keyup handler compares `e.key.toLowerCase()` against `settings.voice.pttKey` but keydown uses `@svelte-put/shortcut` binding — mismatch if pttKey contains uppercase

title: Invite embed auto-fetch triggered by any /invite/XXXXXXXX substring in message content
description: The regex `INVITE_RE = /(?:https?:\/\/[^\s]+)?\/invite\/([A-Za-z0-9]{8})\b/` makes the hostname prefix optional. Any message containing the literal substring `/invite/ABCDEFGH` — regardless of context or origin domain — silently triggers a `GET /invites/{code}` request to the user's current Pulse server. An attacker (another guild member) can craft messages that enumerate valid invite codes on the victim's server by embedding `/invite/XXXXXXXX` strings and observing which ones cause the embed to render (guild name visible to them in the embed card). This is a minor IDOR amplifier: a member who cannot otherwise list invites can use chat to probe invite validity.
recommendation: Make the hostname in INVITE_RE non-optional, requiring a valid `https://` URL prefix (or at minimum the current instance's origin) before treating a path segment as an invite code: `/https?:\/\/[^\s]+\/invite\/([A-Za-z0-9]{8})\b/`. Additionally, restrict the embed fetch to invite codes that match the current active server's origin so deep-link invites from foreign servers do not trigger auto-fetches against the current server.

In `MessageItem.svelte:61`, the regex `INVITE_RE = /(?:https?:\/\/[^\s]+)?\/invite\/([A-Za-z0-9]{8})\b/` has the URL prefix as an optional group (trailing `?`). A bare `/invite/ABCDEFGH` in any message content matches and causes `inviteCode` to be set. This unconditionally renders `<InviteEmbed code={inviteCode} />`, whose `onMount` in `InviteEmbed.svelte` immediately calls `chatApi.getInvitePreview(code)` — which maps to `GET /invites/{code}` against the user's own Pulse server with their auth token. The backend handler (`invites.py:200`) requires `CurrentUser` auth but has no membership check: any authenticated user can call it and learn whether a code is valid plus the guild name, icon URL, and member count. A guild member who cannot list invites (`MANAGE_INVITES`) can craft messages containing `/invite/XXXXXXXX` strings to make other members' clients probe the server for invite validity. The embed card renders the guild name on a 200 response, making valid codes visually distinguishable from invalid ones. No guard in the frontend or backend refutes this path. Severity is correctly assessed as low: the attacker needs to already be a guild member to send such messages, and the leaked information (guild name/icon/member count) is not highly sensitive.

title: store:setAll performs N disk writes instead of one, breaking its atomicity contract
description: The `store:setAll` IPC handler is documented as an 'Atomic batch write — avoids N parallel rename() races' and the preload JSDoc says it 'atomically write[s] multiple key-value pairs in one IPC round-trip'. However the implementation delegates to `storeSet(key, value)` for each entry (line 302), and `storeSet` calls `persist()` every time (store.ts:114). `persist()` does a `writeFileSync` + `renameSync` per call. For N keys, there are N disk writes instead of one. If a write fails mid-batch (e.g., disk full after key 3), the first keys are persisted and later ones are not — the file is left in a partially-updated state, the opposite of the intended guarantee. At maximum all 8 allowed keys would cause 8 separate atomic rename operations.
recommendation: Export a `storeSetBatch(entries: Record<string, unknown>): void` from store.ts that writes all keys into `data` in a loop and calls `persist()` exactly once at the end. Replace the loop in the `store:setAll` handler to call `storeSetBatch` instead of `storeSet` per key.

verdict.reasoning: The code confirms the reviewer's claim exactly. In `desktop/electron/main.ts` lines 293-307, the `store:setAll` handler loops over entries and calls `storeSet(key, value)` for each one (line 302). In `desktop/electron/store.ts`, `storeSet` (lines 108-115) sets `data[key] = value` and then immediately calls `persist()`. `persist()` (lines 51-64) does a `writeFileSync` to a `.tmp` file followed by `renameSync` to the real path on every invocation. So for N keys, there are N separate write+rename cycles. The comment on the IPC handler says "Atomic batch write — avoids N parallel rename() races" and the preload JSDoc (preload.ts:46) says "Atomically write multiple key-value pairs" — both are misleading: the implementation provides N sequential atomic single-key writes, not one atomic multi-key write. A mid-loop I/O error (e.g., disk full after the 3rd key) would leave the first keys persisted and later ones not, which is the opposite of the atomicity guarantee claimed. The fix is straightforward: accumulate all mutations into `data` in a loop and call `persist()` exactly once at the end, either via a new `storeSetBatch` export in store.ts or by inlining the pattern in the handler.

title: Deep-link invite double-delivery on renderer reload when app is already running
description: When `handleDeepLink` fires while the window is visible, it both (a) sets `pendingInvitePayload = payload` and (b) eagerly pushes via `win.webContents.send('pulse:invite', payload)`. The renderer's `onLink` callback navigates to `/invite/[code]`. If the renderer later reloads (Ctrl+R, or any path that remounts the root `+layout.svelte`), `onMount` calls `getPending()` again, `takePendingInvite()` returns the still-buffered payload, and a second navigation to the same invite URL fires. The buffer is only cleared by `takePendingInvite()`, which is never called after the eager push delivers the link. Impact: duplicate invite-page navigation after a renderer reload following a second-instance deep-link.
recommendation: After the eager `webContents.send` at line 97, clear the buffer: set `pendingInvitePayload = null` (or call `takePendingInvite()` and discard the result) so that the pull path via `getPending()` does not re-deliver an already-pushed link.

When `handleDeepLink` is called while the window is visible: (1) `pendingInvitePayload = payload` is set (line 91), and (2) `win.webContents.send('pulse:invite', payload)` is called (line 97). The push delivery (step 2) is received by the `onLink` listener in `+layout.svelte` line 66, which calls `goto(...)` to navigate — but `onLink` only listens on the raw IPC channel and never calls `takePendingInvite()`, so `pendingInvitePayload` remains set. When the renderer reloads, `+layout.svelte`'s `onMount` fires again, calls `getPending()` → IPC `invite:getPending` → `takePendingInvite()` (preload.ts line 91-92, main.ts line 314), which returns the still-buffered payload and triggers a second `goto(...)` navigation. The comment in deeplink.ts lines 89-90 ("The renderer's `invite:getPending` handler clears the buffer so duplicate delivery does not happen") is factually incorrect for the eager-push path — `takePendingInvite()` is only called via the pull path (`invite:getPending` IPC), not by the push path (`pulse:invite` event). The fix is to clear `pendingInvitePayload` (or call `takePendingInvite()`) immediately after the `webContents.send` on line 97.

title: store:setAll triggers N synchronous disk writes instead of one
description: The `store:setAll` IPC handler iterates over the incoming key-value pairs and calls `storeSet(key, value)` for each one. `storeSet` unconditionally calls `persist()`, which serialises the whole blob to JSON and does a `writeFileSync` + `renameSync` (two syscalls) per key. With ALLOWED_STORE_KEYS having 8 entries, a `saveAll()` from the renderer (the normal path in `persistence.ts`) triggers up to 8 sequential synchronous disk writes on the main-process thread. Each write blocks the Electron event loop for the duration of the rename(2). The comment on line 293 says 'avoids N parallel rename() races', implying it was meant to be a single write, but the implementation still loops through `storeSet`.
recommendation: In the `store:setAll` handler, update `data` directly for each key (bypassing `storeSet`) and call `persist()` exactly once after the loop. Either expose a `storeSetMany(entries)` helper in `store.ts` that does this, or inline the mutation and call `persist()` after the for-loop in `main.ts`.

verdict.reasoning: The code in `desktop/electron/main.ts` lines 294-307 confirms the claim exactly. The `store:setAll` IPC handler loops over entries and calls `storeSet(key, value)` for each one. `storeSet` in `store.ts` lines 108-115 unconditionally calls `persist()` after every mutation. `persist()` does `writeFileSync(tmpPath, json)` + `renameSync(tmpPath, storePath)` — two blocking syscalls per key — on the Electron main-process thread. The comment on line 293 ("Atomic batch write — avoids N parallel rename() races") and the matching comment in `persistence.ts` lines 87-88 make the intent clear: a single write. But the implementation calls `storeSet` (which always persists) instead of mutating `data[key]` directly and calling `persist()` once after the loop, so the intent is not fulfilled. With 8 keys in `ALLOWED_STORE_KEYS`, the normal `saveAll()` path from the renderer triggers 8 sequential synchronous disk writes on every debounced save. The bug is real and the recommended fix (accumulate mutations, call `persist()` once) is correct.

title: _isAllowedOrigin re-parses the static TARGET_URL on every navigation/popup event
description: `_isAllowedOrigin` is called from both `will-navigate` and `setWindowOpenHandler`, which fire on every page navigation and every `window.open()` attempt. Each call creates `new URL(TARGET_URL)` even though `TARGET_URL` is a module-level constant whose origin never changes. This is a wasted `URL` parse + allocation on a hot path; the impact is minor in normal use but becomes measurable if the renderer is chatty with `window.open` (e.g. a link-heavy page or a buggy renderer looping).
recommendation: Compute `const TARGET_ORIGIN = new URL(TARGET_URL).origin` once at module scope after `TARGET_URL` is defined, and compare against that constant inside `_isAllowedOrigin` instead of re-parsing `TARGET_URL` each time.

verdict.reasoning: The code at /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/desktop/electron/main.ts lines 210-218 confirms the claim exactly. `_isAllowedOrigin` creates `new URL(TARGET_URL)` (line 213) on every invocation, even though `TARGET_URL` is a module-level constant defined at line 135 whose origin never changes at runtime. The function is wired to both `will-navigate` (line 195) and `setWindowOpenHandler` (line 201). There is no caching of the parsed origin anywhere in the file. The fix — computing `const TARGET_ORIGIN = new URL(TARGET_URL).origin` once at module scope — is valid and trivially applicable. That said, the practical performance impact is extremely minor: `URL` parsing takes microseconds, and these two event handlers fire only on user-initiated navigations or `window.open()` calls in a desktop chat app, not in any tight loop under normal operation. The "measurable" qualifier in the claim requires a pathological renderer (e.g. a buggy loop calling `window.open`), which is unrealistic in this codebase. The finding is real but its severity is correctly rated low.

title: Sidecar binary path env-var overrides not gated on packaged builds
description: PULSE_PYTHON, PULSE_SIDECAR_PY (Linux), and PULSE_HQ_SIDECAR (Windows) are honoured unconditionally, even in a signed/packaged Flatpak or installer build. A malicious .desktop launcher, wrapper script, or Flatpak with write access to the user environment can redirect these to an attacker-controlled executable. That executable receives stream tokens in plaintext via stdin (the start op sends channel.token in the JSON request). By contrast, the analogous PULSE_URL override is explicitly rejected in packaged builds at main.ts:121-133 with a clear comment. The fix is to add the same app.isPackaged guard around all three sidecar path overrides.
recommendation: Wrap the three env-var overrides in sidecar.ts with the same `!app.isPackaged` guard that protects PULSE_URL in main.ts. In a packaged build, skip the env-var check entirely and proceed directly to the walk-up / resourcesPath / Flatpak-default resolution. Document the overrides as dev-only in a comment, matching the PULSE_URL treatment.

In sidecar.ts: PULSE_PYTHON is consumed unconditionally at module load (line 28), PULSE_SIDECAR_PY at resolveScriptPath() lines 101-107, and PULSE_HQ_SIDECAR at resolveBinaryPath() lines 147-153 — none have any app.isPackaged guard. By contrast, main.ts lines 121-133 explicitly gates PULSE_URL with !app.isPackaged and even includes a comment citing "finding 163" and explaining the malicious .desktop threat model. The inconsistency is intentional-looking on the URL side but an oversight on the sidecar side. The attack path is real: a malicious .desktop launcher (e.g. Exec=env PULSE_SIDECAR_PY=/tmp/evil.py flatpak run com.howispulse.Pulse) would cause the sidecar manager to spawn the attacker's binary, which would then receive stream tokens in plaintext JSON via stdin (the start op sends channel.token). On Windows, PULSE_HQ_SIDECAR wins even over the packaged resourcesPath lookup because the env-var branch is checked first (line 147 precedes the resourcesPath check at line 160). Severity is medium rather than high because stream tokens are short-lived (4h TTL), scoped per-channel, and do not expose user credentials or session tokens — the impact is limited to stream hijacking rather than full account compromise.

title: gsr:call IPC handler forwards arbitrary op strings to the sidecar with no allowlist
description: The ipcMain.handle('gsr:call') handler passes the op string and params object to getSidecar().call() without any validation against a known-good op list. The preload's exposed API surface is limited to hard-coded method names (health, gpuInfo, listProfiles, listMonitors, listApplicationAudio, buildArgv, start, stop), which constrains the attack surface for XSS on the loaded origin. However, if an XSS or a future preload change introduces a raw call(op, params) passthrough, an attacker gains the ability to invoke any op the sidecar understands — including future ops that may have wider side effects — and to send arbitrary params (including injected channel/token fields) to the sidecar subprocess stdin. The params spread (sidecar.ts:256) is unchecked beyond `typeof params === 'object'`.
recommendation: Add an ALLOWED_GSR_OPS allowlist (Set of strings) in main.ts before the gsr:call handler and return {ok: false, error: 'unknown op'} for any op not in the list. The set should contain exactly the ops declared in pulse.d.ts: health, gpu_info, list_profiles, list_monitors, list_application_audio, build_argv, start, stop, state.

verdict.reasoning:
The code confirms the factual claim: `ipcMain.handle('gsr:call', ...)` at main.ts:235 passes `op` and `params` to `getSidecar().call()` with no allowlist, while the store handler immediately below it does have `ALLOWED_STORE_KEYS` (lines 254-263). The reviewer's description of the code is accurate.

However, the current exploitability is limited. The preload (preload.ts) exposes only hard-coded named methods via `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld` (`health`, `gpuInfo`, `listProfiles`, `listMonitors`, `listApplicationAudio`, `buildArgv`, `start`, `stop`) — the `gsrCall(op, params)` helper is an internal preload-local function, not exposed to the renderer world. With `contextIsolation: true` and `sandbox: true` set (main.ts lines 169-171), the renderer cannot access `ipcRenderer` directly, so an XSS in the web content cannot invoke `gsr:call` with an arbitrary op string today.

The finding is a real defense-in-depth gap — the `gsr:call` IPC handler is more permissive than it needs to be, and unlike the analogous `store:set` handler (which has an explicit allowlist), it has none. The risk is that a future preload change adding a raw `call(op, params)` passthrough (or any other future preload surface expansion) would silently grant full sidecar op access. The asymmetry with the store handler's allowlist makes this an inconsistent security posture. Severity is appropriately medium: not currently exploitable from the renderer, but a meaningful hardening gap given the existing pattern in the codebase.

title: notify:show IPC handler uses renderer-supplied payload fields without runtime type checks
description: The notify:show handler destructures title, body, channel_id, guild_id, and message_id from the renderer-supplied payload and passes them directly to new Notification({title, body}) and into the NotifyClickPayload without validating that these fields are actually strings at runtime (TypeScript types are erased at runtime). A compromised renderer, or a future XSS on the loaded origin, can send null, a number, or an object for any field. Passing a non-string title/body to Electron's Notification constructor has undefined behaviour across platforms; on some Linux notification daemons it causes the notification daemon to crash or log unexpected content. The channel_id/message_id fields forwarded in the click event are used by the renderer to navigate — sending a crafted non-string value could produce a navigation to an unexpected route.
recommendation: Add explicit runtime type guards at the top of the notify:show handler: check that payload is a non-null object, and that title, body, channel_id, and message_id are strings. Clamp title to ≤256 chars and body to ≤1024 chars. Return the id early (no-op) if validation fails.

verdict.reasoning:
The code at desktop/electron/notify.ts lines 89-103 confirms the finding: payload.title, payload.body, payload.channel_id, payload.guild_id, and payload.message_id are destructured and used without any runtime type checks. The reviewer's claim is accurate.

Mitigating factors that reduce severity: (1) main.ts lines 168-170 show contextIsolation: true, nodeIntegration: false, sandbox: true — the strongest Electron security posture. An attacker in the renderer can only call functions exposed via contextBridge. (2) The app loads a first-party origin (howispulse.com); an XSS there would be a much larger incident. (3) The preload's notify.show forwards the payload as-is (preload.ts line 106) without checking types, but the preload's onClick handler (lines 114-126) does have explicit defensive type checks, showing the author was aware of the need for IPC payload validation in one direction but missed it for the inbound show path.

The finding is real: a crafted non-string value (null, number, object) for title or body reaches new Notification({title, body}) in the Electron main process. Platform behavior for non-string title/body is undefined and can result in unexpected daemon output or coercion on Linux (libnotify). The channel_id/message_id forwarded in the click event back to the renderer do pass through the preload's onClick handler which already validates them (lines 117-120), so the navigation-confusion sub-claim is partially mitigated at the renderer receipt side, though the main process still stores and forwards unvalidated values.

The adjusted severity is low (not medium/high): the realistic exploit requires an XSS on the loaded first-party origin or a compromised preload, and the practical impact of passing null/object to Notification is coercion or a no-op rather than a critical security breach.

title: Self-host Caddyfile uses `handle` (not `handle_path`): API prefix is never stripped
description: Every API block uses Caddy's `handle /api/auth/*`, `handle /api/chat/*`, `handle /api/voice/*`, `handle /api/media/*`. In Caddy 2, `handle` forwards the full path to the upstream; it does NOT strip the matched prefix. The backend services (auth on :8001, chat-gateway on :8002, etc.) register routes at bare paths like `/login`, `/guilds`, `/ws`. When Caddy forwards a request for `/api/chat/guilds` to `127.0.0.1:8002`, the service receives `/api/chat/guilds` instead of `/guilds`, which has no matching route, returning a 404. Every API call on a self-hosted instance silently fails. The cloud/prod nginx config correctly uses `rewrite ^/api/chat/(.*)$ /$1 break;` to strip the prefix; the self-host equivalent must use `handle_path /api/chat/*` (which strips the matched prefix before forwarding).
recommendation: Replace `handle /api/auth/*`, `handle /api/chat/*`, `handle /api/voice/*`, `handle /api/media/*` with `handle_path /api/auth/*` etc. in Caddyfile.template. `handle_path` strips the matched prefix so auth-svc receives `/login` instead of `/api/auth/login`.

verdict.reasoning: The bug is confirmed by reading the actual code. In `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/infra/self-host/s6/etc/caddy/Caddyfile.template`, lines 50-79, every API block uses `handle /api/auth/*`, `handle /api/chat/*`, `handle /api/voice/*`, and `handle /api/media/*` with plain `reverse_proxy`. In Caddy 2, `handle` does not strip the matched prefix before forwarding — only `handle_path` does that. There are no `uri strip_prefix`, `rewrite`, or any other path-stripping directives anywhere in the file (confirmed by grep). The backend services register routes at bare paths: auth-svc at `/login`, `/register`, `/me`, etc. (confirmed in `services/auth/src/dcc_auth/routes.py`); chat-gateway at `/guilds`, `/channels`, etc. (confirmed in `services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/routes/`). The frontend constructs URLs with the full prefix (e.g., `${server.hostname}/api/chat/guilds`) confirmed in `web/src/lib/api/client.ts` lines 47-94. The prod nginx in `infra/prod/web-nginx.conf` lines 85, 92, 99, 109 correctly strips prefixes with `rewrite ^/api/chat/(.*)$ /$1 break;`. The self-host Caddyfile has no equivalent. Every API call to a self-hosted instance will 404 because the backend receives the full prefixed path like `/api/chat/guilds` instead of `/guilds`. The fix is to replace `handle` with `handle_path` on all API blocks.

title: Self-host Caddyfile.template missing `handle /ws` route: WebSocket never connects
description: The self-host frontend determines the WebSocket path based on `isCloud`: for a self-hosted server (`isCloud=false`) it connects to `wss://host/ws` directly (see `web/src/lib/ws/gateway-connection.ts:103`). The Caddyfile.template has `handle /api/ws { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8002 }` (line 65) but no `handle /ws`. The `handle /api/ws` block in the Caddyfile is itself unreachable for normal self-host traffic (no client sends to `/api/ws` on self-host).

In gateway-connection.ts line 103, self-host connections (`isCloud=false`) use wsPath `/ws` by default: `this.wsPath = opts.wsPath ?? (opts.isCloud ? '/api/ws/ws' : '/ws')`. title: PULSE_INSTANCE_OWNER_ID not validated in 10-check-cloud-creds.sh and not exported in env.sh: self-host has no admin
description: `infra/self-host/.env.example` marks `PULSE_INSTANCE_OWNER_ID` as `[PFLICHT]` (required). title: 08-init-mediamtx.sh fallback config uses wrong `authHTTPExclude` key format (`path:` instead of `action:`)
description: When the MediaMTX template file is missing (lines 60-63 of the fallback heredoc), the generated `authHTTPExclude` uses `- path: ^api/.*` and `- path: ^metrics/.*`. MediaMTX 1.17.1 expects `- action: api`, `- action: metrics`, `- action: pprof` (as used in the production `infra/prod/mediamtx.yml:86-89` and `streaming/server/mediamtx.yml.template`). The auth-hook does return 200 for these paths (it checks for the `channel-` prefix), so the functional impact is limited to extra unnecessary HTTP round-trips from MediaMTX to the auth-hook on every probe.
