The fallback heredoc in `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/infra/self-host/s6/etc/s6-overlay/scripts/08-init-mediamtx.sh` lines 60-62 uses `- path: ^api/.*` and `- path: ^metrics/.*`, while both production configs (`infra/prod/mediamtx.yml:87-89` and `streaming/server/mediamtx.yml.template:71-73`) use the correct `- action: api`, `- action: metrics`, `- action: pprof` format. MediaMTX 1.17.1 uses `action:` keys for `authHTTPExclude`, so the `path:` keys are silently ignored and api/metrics/pprof requests are forwarded to the auth-hook. The auth-hook (`routes.py` line 152-153) has an explicit `_EXCLUDED_ACTIONS = frozenset({"api", "metrics", "pprof"})` check and returns 200 for these actions anyway, so there is no functional breakage — only unnecessary extra HTTP round-trips. Additionally, the fallback heredoc also omits the `pprof` exclusion entirely (only has 2 entries vs. 3 in prod), compounding the issue slightly beyond what the reviewer noted.

title: HLS proxy location lacks proxy_buffering off, adds latency to LL-HLS segment delivery
description: The `/hls/` location forwards MediaMTX low-latency HLS (200 ms segments, 100 ms partial segments). nginx's default `proxy_buffering on` causes nginx to buffer the full response body before forwarding bytes to the client. For LL-HLS, the browser relies on incremental chunk delivery to start decoding before a segment is fully received. With buffering enabled, nginx withholds each part until the full proxy response is accumulated in memory, adding up to one round-trip latency (on top of the 100 ms part duration). The MinIO `/pulse-attachments/` location already has `proxy_buffering off` for the same reason (streaming uploads/downloads); the HLS location was not given the same treatment.
recommendation: Add `proxy_buffering off;` to the `/hls/` location block (line 169), mirroring what is already done for the `/pulse-attachments/` location. No other changes are needed.

verdict.reasoning: Reading /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/infra/prod/web-nginx.conf confirms the claim exactly. The `/hls/` location (lines 169-172) has no `proxy_buffering` directive, so nginx's default `proxy_buffering on` applies. In contrast, the `/pulse-attachments/` MinIO location (lines 137-149) explicitly sets both `proxy_request_buffering off` and `proxy_buffering off`. There is no other guard or override that would disable buffering for the HLS location. MediaMTX 1.17.1 (pinned per project config) supports LL-HLS with partial segments; nginx buffering accumulates the full proxy response body before forwarding bytes to the client, which directly defeats LL-HLS's chunked incremental delivery model. The impact is real: each partial segment would be withheld until fully received by nginx, adding latency equal to the partial-segment duration (~100ms per the claim) on top of normal round-trip time. The fix (adding `proxy_buffering off;` to the `/hls/` block) is straightforward and mirrors existing practice in the same file.

title: MinIO backup two-step (mc mirror to named volume + restic) permanently doubles attachment storage
description: The `snapshot_minio` function first runs `mc mirror local/pulse-attachments /var/cache/pulse-backup/minio` (writing the full bucket to the `pulse_minio_stage` named volume) and then invokes `restic backup` against that local copy. The stage volume is persistent and always holds a full mirror of the bucket. As a result the host disk must hold three copies of attachment data simultaneously: the MinIO data volume, the stage mirror, and the restic repository (which deduplicates, but still stores all unique chunks). On a production instance with large attachment stores this can exhaust disk space and the every-6-hours mc mirror run reads the entire changed dataset from MinIO into the stage volume, doubling network I/O inside the Docker network for each backup cycle.
recommendation: Use `restic`'s built-in rclone or S3 backend to back up MinIO directly (`restic -r rclone:local:pulse-attachments backup` or point restic at an S3 remote), eliminating the intermediate stage volume entirely. If the current two-step approach must be kept, mount `pulse_minio_stage` as a `tmpfs` volume so the mirror is not persisted between backup runs, reducing permanent disk overhead to just the MinIO data volume plus the restic repo.

verdict.reasoning:
The code confirms the reviewer's core claim. At /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/infra/prod/backup/backup.sh lines 42-51, `snapshot_minio()` runs `mc mirror --overwrite --remove --quiet local/pulse-attachments /var/cache/pulse-backup/minio` and then `restic backup /var/cache/pulse-backup/minio`. The stage path `/var/cache/pulse-backup` is mounted from the named volume `pulse_minio_stage` (docker-compose.yml line 161, volume declared at line 397 with no special driver options — it is a standard persistent volume, not tmpfs). This means the host disk permanently holds: (1) `pulse_minio` — live MinIO data, (2) `pulse_minio_stage` — a full persistent mirror of the bucket, and (3) `pulse_backups` — the restic repository. That is three copies of attachment data as claimed.

One nuance: the reviewer says each 6-hour run "reads the entire changed dataset from MinIO into the stage volume." The `--overwrite --remove` flags on mc mirror make the run incremental (only changed/new/deleted files sync), so network I/O per run is not the full bucket — only the delta. The doubling-of-network-I/O framing is therefore slightly overstated for typical runs after the first sync. However the permanent disk footprint issue — that `pulse_minio_stage` is a persistent named volume always holding a full copy of all attachments — is exactly as described and fully confirmed by the code. The severity is real: on a large attachment store this doubles the storage cost of just MinIO alone before the restic repo is even counted.

title: /.well-known regex proxy location missing Connection "" header, forces upstream connection close on each CRL/JWKS poll
description: The `/.well-known/` regex location (line 124) proxies JWKS/CRL/suspended-instances endpoints to the `auth` container but omits `proxy_set_header Connection "";`. Without this header, nginx forwards whatever `Connection` value the upstream caller (Caddy or the self-host poller) sent — typically `keep-alive`, but the absence of the explicit override means the upstream HTTP/1.1 keep-alive is not reliably negotiated, potentially closing the connection after each response. All three regular API locations (`/api/auth/`, `/api/chat/`, `/api/voice/`) explicitly set `Connection ""` to enable persistent connections to uvicorn. The well-known location, which is polled periodically by every self-hosted instance for CRL and JWKS updates, was not given the same treatment. Under load (many self-host instances polling frequently) this causes per-request TCP teardown and reconnect to auth-svc.
recommendation: Add `proxy_set_header Connection "";` to the `/.well-known/` regex location block, consistent with the other API proxy locations.

verdict.reasoning: The code confirms the issue exactly. At the server level (lines 65-70), `proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;` is set, where `$connection_upgrade` resolves to `close` for any request without an `Upgrade` header (the map at lines 24-27 maps an empty `$http_upgrade` to `close`). The three regular API locations (`/api/auth/` line 87, `/api/chat/` line 94, `/api/voice/` line 111) each explicitly add `proxy_set_header Connection "";` to override this and enable persistent HTTP/1.1 keep-alive to their upstream containers. The `/.well-known/` regex location (lines 124-128) does not add this override, so every request to it forwards `Connection: close` to auth-svc, causing connection teardown after each response. Caddy or self-host pollers hitting JWKS/CRL/suspended-instances endpoints each get a fresh TCP connection to auth-svc. The finding is accurate and the fix (adding `proxy_set_header Connection "";` to the well-known block) is the correct remedy consistent with the other API locations. Severity of low is appropriate since this only affects periodic background polls, not interactive user requests.

title: X-Forwarded-For spoofing bypasses rate-limit IP bucketing
description: Caddy's bare `reverse_proxy pulse_web:80` appends to (rather than replaces) the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header. A malicious client sends `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4`; Caddy appends the real client IP; nginx then appends its own IP via `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`. The auth service's `_client_ip()` (routes.py:616-623) trusts XFF from any peer in the `TRUSTED_PROXIES` subnet (nginx's container IP is in that /24) and takes the **first** value, which is the attacker-injected `1.2.3.4`. All rate-limit buckets (login, registration, TOTP, WebAuthn) use `_client_ip` as their key, so an attacker can spread brute-force attempts across arbitrary fake IPs to avoid their real IP being blocked.
recommendation: In the Caddyfile block, add `header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}` inside the `reverse_proxy` directive to strip any client-supplied XFF and set only the real remote address. Alternatively, add a Caddy `trusted_proxies` global option so Caddy itself validates its upstream and only trusts the rightmost XFF entry.

verdict.reasoning:
The exploit chain is fully confirmed by the actual code:

1. `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/infra/prod/Caddyfile.pulse.snippet` (line 27): bare `reverse_proxy pulse_web:80` with no `header_up` directive. Caddy 2's reverse_proxy by default appends the connecting client's IP to X-Forwarded-For rather than stripping and replacing it, so a client-supplied `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` header is forwarded downstream with Caddy appending the real client IP.

2. `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/infra/prod/web-nginx.conf` (line 67): `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` — nginx's `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` appends `$remote_addr` (Caddy's container IP) to whatever XFF it received, resulting in `1.2.3.4, <real-client-ip>, <caddy-ip>`.

3. `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/auth/src/dcc_auth/routes.py` (lines 605-623): `_client_ip()` takes `xff.split(",")[0].strip()` — the first/leftmost value — when the peer is trusted. This returns the attacker-injected `1.2.3.4`.

4. `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/auth/src/dcc_auth/config.py` (line 181): `trusted_proxies` defaults to `127.0.0.1,::1`, but `.env.example` line 81 shows the production setting is `TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1,::1,10.0.6.0/24` — the entire pulse-net docker bridge subnet. Auth-svc's immediate peer is the nginx (pulse_web) container whose IP is in that /24. So `_peer_is_trusted()` returns True for all nginx-forwarded requests, and the spoofed first XFF value is used as the rate-limit bucket key.

All rate-limit buckets (login, registration, TOTP, WebAuthn) call `_check_rate()` → `_client_ip()`, so all are bypassable. The fix is to add `header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}` in the Caddy reverse_proxy block to strip and replace the header with only the real remote address.

title: SRT enabled on MediaMTX while stream tokens are transmitted in cleartext over UDP
description: The production MediaMTX config enables SRT on port 8890 (`srt: yes`, `srtAddress: :8890`). The UFW comment in DEPLOY.md lists `8890/udp` as a public ingest port. SRT uses UDP with no built-in TLS, so the stream-token would travel in the `streamid` field in plaintext. Although media-svc currently enforces `protocol: pattern=r"^rtmp$"` (rejecting SRT token issuance via the API), any client who already holds a valid RTMPS token could manually connect via SRT with that token in the `streamid` field before the token is consumed. A passive network observer (ISP or same LAN) could read the token off UDP traffic. The token is single-use (atomically deleted by the auth-hook Lua GETDEL), but the cleartext exposure window still exists during the auth handshake.
recommendation: Disable SRT at the MediaMTX layer (`srt: no` in mediamtx.yml) or close port 8890 at UFW if SRT is not needed. If SRT is needed in future, issue separate SRT-only short-lived tokens and document the no-TLS risk. The current mismatch between the enabled transport (SRT) and the API-level block is a defence-in-depth gap.

verdict.reasoning: The claim is substantiated by the actual code. SRT is enabled in `infra/prod/mediamtx.yml` (line 80: `srt: yes`, `srtAddress: :8890`) and UFW opens 8890/udp. The API-level guard in `services/media-svc/src/dcc_media_svc/routes.py` (line 83) uses `pattern=r"^rtmp$"` to block issuance of SRT push URLs — confirmed. However, the auth-hook in `services/mediamtx-auth-hook/src/dcc_mediamtx_auth_hook/routes.py` does NOT validate the `protocol` field from the stored token record during publish-auth: it only checks `scope`, `channel_id`, `user_id`, and `nonce` (lines 168–187). The token record stored in Redis does carry a `protocol` field (routes.py line 153), but the hook ignores it. This means a client holding a valid RTMP-issued token can present it to the SRT endpoint — the hook will accept it — and during the SRT auth handshake the token travels in the `streamid` field over UDP without TLS encryption. The single-use (Lua GETDEL) semantics limit this to a one-time exposure window, but a passive network observer on the path between the GSR sidecar and the server (ISP, same LAN, or cloud provider network tap) can read the token off the UDP packet before the auth-hook consumes it. The code comment in routes.py line 81–82 ("SRT is disabled: UDP has no TLS layer so the stream token would be visible in cleartext") acknowledges the risk but the mitigation is incomplete: the SRT listener remains open and the auth-hook doesn't enforce the protocol restriction. Severity is appropriately medium: the token is single-use and 32 bytes of urlsafe entropy, but the cleartext exposure is real and SRT on 8890/udp is publicly reachable per DEPLOY.md.

title: MediaMTX API bound to 0.0.0.0:9997 with no authentication, protected only by UFW host firewall
description: The MediaMTX control API (`api: yes`, `apiAddress: :9997`) binds all host interfaces, including any Docker bridge addresses. Access is restricted only by a UFW rule (`ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 9997`). The MediaMTX API has no built-in authentication. If the UFW rule is accidentally removed, misconfigured, or bypassed (e.g., by a container with `network_mode: host` that the API itself runs under), the API is reachable from the public internet. Via the API an attacker could enumerate active streams, kick publishers, and manipulate paths. Additionally, UFW operates on iptables, which Docker's DNAT rules can bypass for bridge-network containers (as noted in the compose file comment about pulse_web binding to loopback).
recommendation: Bind the MediaMTX API to loopback only (`apiAddress: 127.0.0.1:9997`) if media-svc can reach it via `host.docker.internal` mapping to the gateway IP rather than `127.0.0.1`. If that is not possible with the current host-network setup, add `apiAllowAddresses` allowlist in mediamtx.yml to accept connections only from the Docker bridge gateway. Document in DEPLOY.md that this UFW rule is security-critical and must be verified after any network reconfiguration.

verdict.reasoning:
The core finding is real: `apiAddress: :9997` in `infra/prod/mediamtx.yml:73` binds the MediaMTX API on all host interfaces with no built-in authentication, and the sole access control is a UFW rule (`ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 9997`). This is confirmed and explicitly documented in the config itself (lines 66–71) as a deliberate trade-off because `media-svc` reaches MediaMTX via `host.docker.internal` (the Docker bridge gateway, not loopback), so binding to `127.0.0.1` would break the stream-state poller.

However, the reviewer's central exploit amplification — that Docker's DNAT rules can bypass UFW for this port — is incorrect for this specific case. MediaMTX runs with `network_mode: host` (docker-compose.yml:354), so it binds port 9997 directly on the host kernel stack with no Docker DNAT/port-mapping involved. The Docker DNAT bypass issue (explicitly noted in docker-compose.yml:319–323) only applies to bridge-network containers with published ports. For host-network services, UFW's `INPUT` chain does govern the traffic normally.

The actual residual risk is: if the UFW rule is accidentally removed or a misconfiguration occurs, port 9997 is openly reachable from the internet with no authentication, allowing stream enumeration and publisher management. This is a real defense-in-depth gap. The design is acknowledged and documented, but loopback binding would eliminate the risk entirely — except that doing so requires an architectural change (e.g., binding to the specific Docker bridge gateway IP instead of loopback, so `host.docker.internal` from `media-svc` can still connect). The severity is medium as claimed, but the Docker-DNAT bypass angle is not a valid exploit path here.

title: INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET defaults to empty in .env.example, disabling ban/kick voice eviction silently
description: The `.env.example` ships with `INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET=` (empty). When this is left unset in production, `POST /internal/evict-from-voice` (voice-signaling) returns 401 with detail `internal endpoint disabled`. The comment warns about this, but it is easy to overlook. The concrete impact: when an admin bans or kicks a user who is currently in a LiveKit voice channel, the chat-gateway call to evict them from voice silently fails with 401. The banned/kicked user remains connected to the voice channel until they disconnect voluntarily, despite the ban taking effect for all other channels. The account-deletion flow also becomes unavailable (DELETE /me returns 503).
recommendation: Add a startup check in chat-gateway and voice-signaling that logs a prominent WARNING if `INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET` is empty. Better: use a compose-level `:?required` guard (`INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET=${INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET:?INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET required}`) to make deployment fail fast, with a note in DEPLOY.md on how to generate it. The current comment warns operators, but a hard failure at deploy time is safer.

verdict.reasoning: The code confirms the finding. In `/infra/prod/.env.example:68`, `INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET=` is empty. In `services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/voice_evict.py:43-46`, when `secret` is falsy (empty string), `evict_user_from_guild_voice` logs at INFO level and returns immediately — the HTTP call to voice-signaling is never made. Result: when an admin bans or kicks a user currently in a LiveKit voice channel, voice eviction is silently skipped. The banned/kicked user remains in the voice channel until they disconnect voluntarily. The `DELETE /me` account-deletion path (`routes_account.py:116`) is also disabled. The reviewer's minor error is the HTTP status code — they said 401 but it would actually be 503 on the voice-signaling side — however this is moot because chat-gateway short-circuits before making the request at all. There are no startup guards or hard-fail checks in any service that would alert an operator. The `.env.example` comment warns about this at lines 65-67, but only as a text warning, not a deployment-time failure. The impact path is real and reachable in any production deployment that copies `.env.example` without setting this value.
